clue.text: French castrated male broken by laser treatment

indicators.note: the word laser gets treated, worked over into a new order of its letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A neutered Frenchman whose condition is worsened by a course of laser therapy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' looks like an adjective for the castrated male, but on its own it is the definition: French is slang for the act.
explanation.definitionFit: In bawdy slang, French refers to oral sex, from the old stereotype of French erotic habits.

clue.text: United to get Bill and Jonathan? Here's a starter clue

parts.note: joined together, made one
AC stands for account, a bill
Jonathan Ross is a British chat-show host

explanation.surface: A football club hoping to sign two players, and a crossword hint offered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'United' suggests a football team; it means made one.
explanation.definitionFit: One Across is the opening clue of most crosswords, the one solvers start on.

clue.text: Rupert's mate said "Pond life!"

parts.note: Algy Pug is a friend of Rupert Bear in the comic strip

explanation.surface: A friend of Rupert Bear sneers at someone as pond life.
explanation.walkthrough: Rupert Bear is a long-running British children's comic character; his chum Algy is a pug dog.
explanation.definitionFit: Algae are simple plants that grow as green scum in ponds, a basic form of pond life.

clue.text: Pose Mozart incongruously with a load of fertilisers

indicators.note: arranged in an unsuitable way, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A farmer posing Mozart absurdly among sacks of fertiliser.
explanation.definitionFit: Spermatozoa are male reproductive cells, and a load of them is an ejaculation that fertilises eggs.

clue.text: Zealous quiz-master of interest to blokes getting it up outside

definitions.note: the crossword setter took his pseudonym from a Spanish Inquisitor

in a down clue, getting it up means the word is read from the bottom

parts.note: it is a coy word for sex

explanation.surface: A keen quiz host whose programme appeals to men with erections.
explanation.walkthrough: Ximenes was the pseudonym of D. S. Macnutt, the Observer crossword setter, named after Cardinal Ximenes, a zealous Grand Inquisitor.
explanation.definitionFit: The setter Ximenes posed fiendish puzzles each week, and his chosen name came from a fanatical Inquisitor.

clue.text: Thatcher-style negotiating tool: giving worker the sack!

parts.note: a hand is a manual worker, as in farmhand
a sack is a large bag

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher's bargaining weapon was firing staff, the cliché about her union-bashing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Giving worker the sack' reads as dismissal, but it simply sets one piece beside the other. Thatcher was famed for 'handbagging' ministers and EU partners.
explanation.definitionFit: Margaret Thatcher's ever-present accessory became a byword for her bruising way of negotiating, hence the verb handbag.

clue.text: Sand dancing during Little Darling's one sort of learning technique

definitions.note: the answer works as an adjective here, one sort of technique

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A child dancing on the sand as a way of learning.
explanation.definitionFit: Hands-on learning means practical, direct experience rather than theory.

clue.text: Freak sperm producer

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a testicle, in crude slang

explanation.walkthrough: One short slang word covers an obsessive fan and a testicle.
explanation.definitionFit: Nut is slang both for a fanatic or crank and for a testicle, which produces sperm.

clue.text: Blairs can change English for Italian hangers-on

definitions.note: plural noun, matching the plural answer

indicators.note: the letters are altered into a different order
one letter takes the place of another

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The Blair family could swap their English friends for Italian ones, a jab at holidays with Berlusconi.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' is part of the fodder as well as the anagram signal's partner: Blairs plus can gives the letters once Italian is swapped for English.
explanation.definitionFit: Barnacles cling to ships' hulls, so the word figuratively means persistent hangers-on.

clue.text: Puffs talk about turning over police sergeant

parts.note: to gas about something is to chatter on about it

explanation.surface: Someone chatting about overturning a police sergeant, puffing as they go.
explanation.walkthrough: The words 'turning over' add nothing to the letters, which come out in clue order; they appear to be surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: Gasps are short sharp intakes of breath, the same as puffs when panting.

clue.text: Headless mutt's hole

indicators.note: the dog's name loses its front letter, its head

parts.note: a beagle is a breed of dog, a mutt; the 's is read as 'is'

explanation.surface: A dog with no head and a hole in it: a grisly little image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hole' looks like a pit, but here it is a golf hole.
explanation.definitionFit: An eagle is a golf score of two under par on a hole, so the hole is named for the score.

clue.text: Fighters meant to get revitalised members (connectors inserted)

indicators.note: brought back to life in a new form, so the letters of meant are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
arms are limbs, members of the body

explanation.surface: Soldiers expected to have their limbs restored, with joints fitted in between.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed '(connectors inserted)' is a jokey nod to the two hyphens in the answer, not part of the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Men-at-arms were medieval soldiers, so the phrase names fighters, especially armoured ones.

clue.text: The best singles Frenchman's orgasm

parts.note: the cream is the finest part of anything
ones are single units

explanation.surface: A French pop fan enjoying the hit parade a little too much.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The best singles' suggests a pop chart, but it splits into two separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: To cream one's jeans is crude slang for having an orgasm while clothed, often from excitement.

clue.text: See 11
Roy Webb jacked off missing journalist? That's a load of balls

indicators.note: gone wrong, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.walkthrough: 'Jacked off' looks like a crude verb; 'off' is the signal and 'jacked' loses its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem gave English a word for meaningless gibberish, which is what balls means in slang.

clue.text: Knocker-off of old lady's stereo's out of order

indicators.note: broken and jumbled, so the letters of stereo's are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Someone who has nicked a pensioner's sound system, which no longer works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Knocker-off' suggests a thief; in Greek myth Orestes killed (knocked off) his mother Clytemnestra.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek legend Orestes avenged his father Agamemnon by slaying his mother, the old lady of the clue.

clue.text: Loosened the belt to accommodate Brenda, our old monarch

slackened, so the letters of the belt fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Private Eye's nickname for the Queen, who is ER

explanation.surface: Easing a belt to make room for the Queen.
explanation.walkthrough: Ethelbert, King of Kent, was baptised by St Augustine; 'our old monarch' is an English king of long ago.
explanation.definitionFit: Ethelbert was an Anglo-Saxon king of Kent, an English ruler from about AD 600.

clue.text: Penis, having lost tip, was bloody prevented from getting a proper ride

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ride' looks sexual, but it is a jockey's ride: a nobbled racehorse has been tampered with so it cannot run properly.
explanation.definitionFit: To nobble a horse is to drug or injure it so that it cannot race well, denying its jockey a fair run.

clue.text: Makes you spit being surrounded by plonkers, nerds, etc.

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Being stuck among idiots and geeks makes you want to spit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'you' only joins the surface: the four letters of spit go inside the slang word.
explanation.definitionFit: Dipstick is mild slang for a fool, which nerds and similar types are being called.

clue.text: In lively movements, Brenda's going for one's nuts, put brutally

definitions.note: a plural noun: people who are nuts, named in a crude, unkind way

parts.note: scherzos are brisk, playful movements in symphonies and sonatas
Private Eye calls the Queen Brenda, and the Queen is ER; the 's is read as 'is'
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: The Queen has lost her mind during a lively piece of music.
explanation.walkthrough: Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth II, so it gives ER.
explanation.definitionFit: Schizo is an offensive slang term for someone thought mad, a brutal way of calling people nuts.

clue.text: To be an MP (promiscuous), don't budge off your arse

fast in the old sense of loose-living

explanation.surface: Advice to a randy MP: stay put and don't get up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Off your arse' is British slang for off your bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: To sit fast means to stay firmly where you are and refuse to move.

clue.text: To pissed reps, booze equals exercise

indicators.note: drunk, so the letters of reps stagger into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
to sup is to drink

explanation.definitionFit: A press-up is a gym exercise, lowering and raising the body with the arms; Americans call it a push-up.

explanation.walkthrough: A wigging is a British word for a scolding; here it is read literally as being fitted with a wig.

taken as the word and

explanation.walkthrough: 'Fanny' looks like a woman's name, but in British slang it means the female genitals.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny is British slang for the female genitals, which the anatomical term names.

clue.text: Our Tony's number one estate?

the clergy are the First Estate of the realm, so a parson belongs to it

explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye's long-running spoof 'St Albion Parish News' featured Tony Blair as the trendy vicar.

clue.text: Overreact, giving it what for

clue.text: Knocking off Art, a wifeless pillock

clue.text: Matter-of-fact way of saying "It's subject to prohibition, head"
